items.label: Research question
items.prompt: This article states its research question as an actual QUESTION. Find it.
items.model: How does Facebook usage influence subjective well-being over time?
items.why: A literal question in the Introduction ('So, how does…?') is the research question.

items.label: Hypothesis
items.prompt: Do the authors state a hypothesis about the direction of the effect?
options: Yes: Facebook use will lower well-being
Yes: Facebook use will raise well-being
No: findings are mixed, so only a question is asked
items.ans: No: findings are mixed, so only a question is asked
items.model: No hypothesis: earlier findings were mixed (some positive, some negative), so the study is framed as an open question.
items.why: When the literature is mixed, authors may ask an open research question instead of predicting a direction.

items.label: Research gap
items.prompt: Find the sentence stating the research gap.
items.model: No research has examined how Facebook use influences subjective well-being OVER TIME.
items.why: The gap is stated early and supported by a review of 412 publications.

items.label: Why a new design?
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining why previous studies CAN'T answer the question.
items.model: Previous studies were cross-sectional, so it's impossible to know the direction over time.
items.why: This links the gap to the choice of an experience-sampling (lagged) design.

items.label: Two components of well-being
items.prompt: Find the sentence (in the Introduction) that names the TWO components of subjective well-being being studied.
items.model: Affective well-being (how people feel) and cognitive well-being (how satisfied they are with their lives).
items.why: These two components become the two outcome variables.

items.label: Operational definition (affect)
items.prompt: Find the first part of the text-message question that measured AFFECT.
items.model: 'How do you feel right now?' on a slider from very positive (0) to very negative (100).
items.why: Note the direction: HIGHER scores = more NEGATIVE feelings. This matters when you read the B values.

items.label: Operational definition (direct interaction)
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining what counted as interacting 'DIRECTLY'.
items.model: Face-to-face or phone interactions.
items.why: Operational definitions can be hidden in the procedure.

items.label: General method
items.prompt: Which best describes the design?
items.model: Experience sampling with lagged analyses; nothing was manipulated.
items.why: Timing helps suggest a causal order, but without manipulation it's still correlational. The authors admit experiments are needed.

items.label: Sample
items.prompt: Find the sentence describing the participants.
items.model: 82 people (mean age 19.52; 53 female; mostly European American) recruited via flyers in Ann Arbor, Michigan.
items.why: Demographics and recruitment are in one long sentence.

items.label: Data exclusion
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining whose data were EXCLUDED for low response rates.
items.model: Two participants who responded to fewer than 33% of texts were excluded (4,589 observations left).
items.why: Data cleaning decisions are often reported at the start of the Results.

items.label: Affective well-being result
items.prompt: Find the result showing that Facebook use predicted worse feelings later.
items.model: The more people used Facebook, the worse they subsequently felt, B = .08, p < .0001.
items.why: Remember the affect scale: higher = more negative, so a POSITIVE B means feeling worse.

items.label: Reverse direction
items.prompt: Find the result showing that feelings did NOT predict later Facebook use.
items.model: T1 affect did not predict later Facebook use, p = .82.
items.why: Testing the reverse path helps rule out 'feeling bad makes people use Facebook'.

items.label: Alternative explanation
items.prompt: Find the sentence stating the FIRST alternative explanation the authors tested.
items.model: Maybe ANY form of social interaction undermines well-being.
items.why: They test it by repeating the analyses with direct social interaction instead of Facebook use.

items.label: Ruling it out
items.prompt: Find the result that rules out that first alternative explanation.
items.model: Direct interaction did not predict changes in life satisfaction and predicted feeling BETTER.
items.why: If all social contact were harmful, direct interaction should also predict declines. It didn't.

items.label: Loneliness
items.prompt: Loneliness predicted more Facebook use. Find the sentence showing that controlling for loneliness did NOT remove the Facebook effect.
items.model: Facebook use still predicted declines in both kinds of well-being with loneliness controlled.
items.why: This rules out loneliness as a third variable explaining the result.

items.label: Moderators
items.prompt: Did any of the tested moderators (gender, self-esteem, depression, network size, etc.) change the Facebook effect?
options: No, none of them changed the effect
items.ans: No, none of them changed the effect
items.model: No significant moderation (all ps > .16).
items.why: 'In no case did we observe any significant interactions' means no moderators.

items.label: Exploratory analysis
items.prompt: Find the sentence where the authors admit an analysis had NO prediction beforehand (a priori).
items.model: They had no a priori predictions about the Facebook × direct contact interaction, but explored it anyway.
items.why: Exploratory findings are less trustworthy than tested predictions and should be treated with more caution.

items.label: Possible mechanism
items.prompt: No framework is given in the Introduction. Find where the authors finally mention possible THEORETICAL mechanisms (e.g. social comparison).
items.model: Facebook may interfere with physical activity or trigger damaging social comparisons.
items.why: Here the theory appears only in Future research, as a possible explanation to test, not as a framework that justified a hypothesis.

items.label: Causal claims
items.prompt: Find the sentence where the authors admit experiments are still needed to establish CAUSATION.
items.model: Experiments that manipulate Facebook use are needed to establish definitive causal relations.
items.why: Lagged analyses suggest a likely order, but only experiments can establish cause.

items.label: Effect size caveat
items.prompt: Find the caveat about the SIZE of the effects.
items.model: The effects were statistically significant but small; the authors argue they still matter practically.
items.why: Significance tells you an effect is unlikely to be chance; effect size tells you how big it is.

items.label: Measurement caveat
items.prompt: Find the caveat about how AFFECT was measured.
items.model: A single bipolar good–bad scale may hide whether people felt less positive, more negative, or both.
items.why: This is a measurement limitation; the next sentence suggests the fix for future research.

items.label: Generalisability
items.prompt: Find the sentence raising the question of whether the findings apply to OTHER AGE GROUPS.
items.model: It's important to test whether the findings generalise to other age groups.
items.why: Generalisability limitations can be framed as future research questions.
